title: Holy Sonnet X: context and date
short: One of Donne's Holy Sonnets, numbered X in Grierson's edition, which follows the order of the 1635 printing; probably written c. 1609-10.
body: The poem belongs to the 'Holy Sonnets' (also called 'Divine Meditations'), first printed in 1633. Numbering differs between the early editions and manuscripts; it is commonly called Holy Sonnet X after Grierson, whose first sixteen sonnets follow the order of the 1635 edition (the Westmoreland manuscript, discovered later, has its own sequence). Helen Gardner dated the main group to 1609-10, a period of illness, poverty and religious crisis before Donne's ordination in 1615. Many of the Holy Sonnets meditate on death and judgment with fear; this one instead taunts death with confident faith, though some readers hear the bravado as an attempt to overcome fear.

title: apostrophe to Death
short: Death is addressed as a person and argued down: personification and apostrophe turn a terror into a defeated braggart.
body: The sonnet speaks directly to Death, as one might rebuke a boastful man. Personified Death was familiar from the Dance of Death and from Scripture ('O death, where is thy sting?', 1 Corinthians 15:55, itself echoing Hosea 13:14). 'Some have called thee Mighty and dreadfull' concedes the common opinion before refuting it. The metre of the opening line is notably irregular, giving a strong stress to 'Death' and to 'proud', a roughness Ben Jonson famously criticised in Donne's verse generally.

title: Die not, poore death
short: Those Death thinks it kills do not truly die, because their souls live on; so Death is to be pitied, 'poore death'.
body: The argument rests on the Christian doctrine of the immortality of the soul and the resurrection of the body. 'Poore death' reverses the usual roles: the speaker condescends to Death. 'Nor yet canst thou kill mee' is personal: the speaker's own salvation is the confident ground of the taunt, though some critics note how this confidence contrasts with the anxiety of other Holy Sonnets.

sources.cite: Helen Gardner (ed.), John Donne: The Divine Poems (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1952; 2nd edn 1978), commentary

title: rest and sleepe ... thy pictures
short: Rest and sleep are only images of Death; if they give pleasure, Death, the real thing, must give much more.
body: Sleep as the image or brother of death is a classical commonplace: in Hesiod's Theogony and Homer's Iliad (16.672), Sleep and Death are twin brothers, and the Latin tag 'somnus est imago mortis' was familiar. Donne turns the comparison into an argument a fortiori: since sleep, a mere 'picture', gives pleasure, the original must give 'much more'. 'Pictures' means likenesses or images.

title: soonest our best men
short: The best die soonest, an old proverb ('whom the gods love die young'), here showing that going with Death is a privilege.
body: The thought recalls the classical proverb 'whom the gods love dies young', found in Menander and in Plautus, Bacchides 816 ('quem di diligunt adulescens moritur'). In Christian terms the good are taken early into rest. Donne uses it to argue that Death cannot be dreadful if the best people go with it willingly and soonest. The phrase 'with thee doe goe' presents Death as a travelling companion rather than an executioner.

title: Rest of their bones, and soules deliverie
short: Death gives the body rest and releases the soul from the prison of the flesh, completing the octave's argument.
body: The line is in apposition: going with Death is rest for the bones and 'deliverie' (release, setting free) for the soul. The idea of the body as the soul's prison is Platonic (Phaedo) and Pauline ('who shall deliver me from the body of this death?', Romans 7:24). 'Deliverie' may also carry the sense of childbirth, death as birth into new life, an image Donne uses in his last sermon, Deaths Duell (1631). The archive text has no punctuation at the end of the octave.

title: slave to Fate, chance, kings, and desperate men
short: The sestet's turn: Death is no master but a slave, set to work by fate, accident, executions and suicides.
body: The volta at l. 9 inverts Death's status: far from 'Mighty', Death is the servant of other powers: fate (or Providence), chance accidents, kings who order executions and wars, and 'desperate men', probably men driven to murder or to suicide. Despair was itself a sin, and Donne had examined suicide in Biathanatos (c. 1608). The rhythm of the line, crowded with stresses, is part of its contemptuous force.

title: doth with poyson ... dwell
short: Death lives in low company, with poison, war and disease; the archive text reads 'doth' where most editions print 'dost'.
body: Death keeps degrading company, which further lowers its dignity. The verb in this archive text is 'doth'; Grierson and most modern editions read 'dost', agreeing with 'Thou' in l. 9. The three companions correspond loosely to the agents of the previous line: poison (desperate men), war (kings), sickness (chance or fate). The line therefore extends the list of Death's masters into a list of its low associates, completing the reversal of l. 9.

title: poppie, or charmes
short: Opium and spells can produce sleep as well as Death can, and more gently than Death's 'stroake'.
body: The poppy was the source of opium, used as a sleeping draught; 'charmes' are incantations or spells believed to induce sleep. Death's power to bring sleep is therefore not unique: drugs and magic do as much, and 'better then thy stroake' (stroke, blow), so Death has no reason to 'swell' with pride. The argument returns to the sleep analogy of ll. 5-6: if sleep can be bought from an apothecary, Death's gift is nothing special.

title: swell'st
short: Why do you puff yourself up with pride? Returns to 'be not proud' in l. 1.
body: 'Swell' means to be puffed up with pride or arrogance, a sense common in the period. The rhetorical question closes the logical case against Death and brings the poem back to its opening command. In some readings the swelling also suggests the bloating of a corpse. The question is the last of the poem's arguments before the couplet's statement of faith, so the rhetoric shifts from disputation to proclamation.

title: One short sleepe past
short: Death is only a brief sleep before resurrection and eternal waking; the sleep image of l. 5 returns with Christian meaning.
body: The New Testament speaks of the dead as 'them which are asleep' who will be raised (1 Thessalonians 4:13-17; 1 Corinthians 15:51-52, 'we shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed'). Death is a short sleep between this life and the general resurrection, after which the faithful 'wake eternally'. The line turns the pagan commonplace of sleep as Death's image into the Christian promise of waking.

title: death shall be no more, death thou shalt die
short: The paradoxical close draws on St Paul ('the last enemy ... is death') and Revelation ('there shall be no more death').
body: The final line combines two biblical promises: 'The last enemy that shall be destroyed is death' (1 Corinthians 15:26) and 'there shall be no more death' (Revelation 21:4). The paradox that Death itself will die is ancient in Christian writing (Hosea 13:14, 'O death, I will be thy plagues'). The sonnet thus ends by turning Death's own weapon against it, in the repeated 'death ... death ... die', where Death is killed with its own name.

title: sonnet form
short: A Petrarchan octave (abbaabba) with an English-style sestet (cddcee) ending in a couplet: Donne's usual Holy Sonnet form.
body: The octave rhymes thee / soe / overthrow / mee / bee / flow / goe / deliverie (abbaabba); the sestet men / dwell / well / then / eternally / die (cddcee). The combination of an Italian octave with a closing couplet is characteristic of Donne's Holy Sonnets. The turn at l. 9 shifts from arguing that Death is not dreadful to arguing that it is base, and the couplet delivers the theological conclusion.
